scope_note: Full-source boundary-date probe covering 9 targets and 7 contexts. Complete retained bodies, dates, excluded layers and voices were checked; no links are accepted and broad lower XML bounds are not treated as period knowledge.

record_reviews.summary: The Kent Church Penitentiary Society explains that its small domestic-servant Home received seventy-one women from Kent prisons and satisfactorily dealt with fifty-three, but was too expensive and lacked general support. It reports the decision to close the present Home, transfer the work to a broader refuge model, and asks Darwin for debt relief and an annual subscription. The surviving letter is heavily damaged with missing portions in the opening and resolution.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 21 Feb 1866]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1866-02-20. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming institutional appeal; the Society speaks collectively and asks for donation/subscription.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin request or response is preserved; the appeal does not identify a correspondence pair.

evidence.quote: Since the first formation of “The Home” seventy one cases have been received
We beg respectfully to ask you to co-operate with us by a donation

record_reviews.summary: Kovalevsky discusses sharing profits from Darwin’s new book and earlier four-volume work, the losses caused by Russian pirated abridgements of Descent of Man, and the risk that Expression will likewise be cheaply translated with copied woodcuts. He offers a short visit to arrange the matter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 8 Aug 1872]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1872-08-07. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Kovalevsky letter; Russian publishing and financial concerns are his voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s prior commercial correspondence is missing; the letter is an offer/negotiation, not a matched scientific answer.

evidence.quote: two pirated abridged edition of the same work selling at a very low price
By publishing the work “on Expression” shortly after the original

record_reviews.summary: Lacy’s 83-block questionnaire-and-answer manuscript records observations of Aboriginal expressions: raised eyebrows and vocal sounds for astonishment, limited shame, weapon-clutching anger, frowning while tracking, laughter with tears, grief, contempt, disgust, fear, and affirmative/negative head or word signals. It then gives a long, explicitly local vocabulary list and remarks that some answers were contemporaneous notes while others came from memory. The final generalization and vocabulary remain Lacy’s own, including prejudicial evaluation, not Darwin’s voice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 13 Aug 1868]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1868-08-12. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Lacy report; numbered questions are Darwin’s prompts as reproduced by Lacy, while answers and vocabulary are Lacy’s observations/recollections.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The underlying Darwin questionnaire and any Darwin reply are not preserved here; this cannot be treated as a direct letter pair.

evidence.quote: Astonishment I have seen expressed by the eyebrows’ being raised
With one or two exceptions these were noted down at different times

record_reviews.summary: Lindley answers Darwin’s seed submission: he will report later and keep information from circulating through his agents, but expects little novelty because one seed is Polygonum and the other probably Chenopodium. He identifies the shortcoming as lack of time and closes formally.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [after 8 Apr 1843]; XML bounds 1843-04-09 to 1882-12-31. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Lindley letter; botanical identifications and confidentiality promise are Lindley’s voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s seed-covering letter is not included; no later Darwin response is identified.

evidence.quote: shall find its way into circulation through my agents.
one is certainly a Polygonum, and the other in all probability a Chenopodium

record_reviews.summary: Litchfield critiques Herbert Spencer’s account of musical expression. He accepts Spencer’s treatment of vocal elements but says Spencer overstates it as an explanation of music, emphasizing relative intervals, scale position, common-chord physics, melody, and unanswered questions about why intervals carry emotional character. The manuscript has references to page and line locations and develops a qualified possible clue rather than a settled theory.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 2 Dec 1871]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1871-12-01. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Litchfield memorandum/letter; Spencer is analyzed as a third-party author and musical examples are Litchfield’s argument.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s request or intended use is not preserved; the note is a critique addressed to Darwin but not a traceable answer to a dated prompt.

evidence.quote: The great law about the expression conveyed in music is that it depends wholly on the relations of the sounds to each other
it might be possible to trace in this fact some explanation of the mental effects of certain sequences of sounds

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Lubbock for a dinner invitation but declines because of poor health and says he will not dine out for several weeks or months.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 28 June 1856; XML bounds 1856-06-28 to 1865-01-28. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The invitation is referenced but no separate incoming record is present; no scientific or period pair is inferred.

evidence.quote: I am very much obliged for your invitation to dinner on the 30th

record_reviews.summary: Lynch supplies a diagram-like observational record for Euphorbia jacquiniaeflora: upper leaves are in nocturnal position at 9 p.m., day/night tip distances are marked in red, leaf lengths in pencil, and younger leaves bend through petiole curvature rather than around a centre. The height of the raised leaves varies with light. The retained block is a dense descriptive memorandum with diagram annotations, not an ordinary prose letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 14 Sept 1877]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1877-09-13. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Lynch observational memorandum; red/pencil marks and figure-like labels are source descriptions, not Darwin annotations.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s request and any figure or response endpoint are absent; the note alone does not establish a direct link.

evidence.quote: The younger leaves are subject to sleep by curving of petiole
The height to which the leaves are raised depends on the intensity of light

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Hermann Müller for an essay on bees and wasps, praises the gradation of bee mouth-organs and independent hexagonal cell-building, and encloses a rough account of a Bombus male habit for Müller to investigate. He offers the manuscript for use and hopes Müller will provide further observations.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 5 May 1872]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1872-05-04. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Hermann Müller’s essay is read/reported, while Darwin’s enclosed account and request are his own.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The essay is a referenced prior input but no separate source endpoint is preserved here; this note is an outgoing request, not a response.

evidence.quote: The perfection of the gradation in the character of bees
The males of Bombus follow one remarkable habit

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Müller’s 1 October letter and Oxalis bulbils, discusses irregular stamen abortion and possible sterility, requests Cordia seed, examines Müller’s Mimosa pod-valve drawing and seed resistance to bird gizzards, asks about Maxillaria capsules and Catasetum roots, and reports sending seeds to Kew and copies of Origin and the climbing-plants paper.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 10 Dec 1866]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1866-12-09. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Müller’s observations and drawing are reported as incoming material, with Darwin’s own experimental questions and publication logistics separate.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The full Müller prompt is not present; no exact response edge is asserted from shared plant topics.

evidence.quote: I have received the bulbillas of Oxalis & your most interesting letter of Oct 1st
your account & drawing of the valves of the pod of one of the Mimoseæ

record_reviews.summary: Darwin forwards Lindley unusual seeds found by William Kemp beneath deep sand over an ancient lake margin, asks Lindley to plant them and report privately, and explains Kemp’s wish to publish himself. Royle’s suggestion and Daubeny’s absence are contextual routes, not additional authors of the letter.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Kemp’s discovery is reported and Lindley is the recipient.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Lindley’s later reply is represented by context 669, but 669 has an after-8-April date and the report keeps this boundary relationship unaccepted pending primary adjudication.

evidence.quote: forwarding to you a few seeds, which have been found under very singular circumstances
Mr Kemp is anxious to publish an account of his discovery himself

record_reviews.summary: Lindley acknowledges Darwin’s communications, identifies Gentians as a valuable addition to knowledge of double flowers, reports an ovule nucleus as another growing point, and identifies Darwin’s Scottish seeds as Rumex acetosella and an uncertain Atriplex sent to Henslow.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 2 Sept 1843]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1843-09-01. This boundary-probe record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: incoming Lindley voice; Henslow and the unnamed “others” are recipients of the specimen, not Darwin.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a response to Darwin’s earlier botanical materials, but no new period-specific Darwin reply is preserved.

evidence.quote: a very curious monster found this year near Ely shows the ovule
Your Scotch seeds proved Rumex Acetosella

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Lindley to pass along his South American Geology to the Gardeners’ Chronicle despite its unusual fit, highlights the Patagonia salt passage, and recalls Lindley’s offer of access to the Horticultural Library. He says the note requires no acknowledgement.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [c. 10 Oct 1846]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; the published book and Gardeners’ Chronicle are public/documentary contexts.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No incoming Lindley prompt is preserved and the broad catalogue date is c. 10 October 1846, outside the period probe.

evidence.quote: the exceedingly pure salt of Patagonia not answering well for preserving meat
this note requires no sort of acknowledgement

record_reviews.summary: Darwin reports a long interview with Baugh over the Down School trust dispute. He relays Baugh’s possible Charity Commissioners or Court of Equity actions, the demand for half the fund or £200, and the plan to expose correspondence to a Farnborough vestry. Darwin’s own threats and assessment of Baugh’s resolve are distinguished from Baugh’s statements.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 10 Jan [1855]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing advisory letter to Lubbock; Baugh’s words are reported third-party speech.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Lubbock’s prompt is not included; the legal dispute is not a scientific correspondence pair.

evidence.quote: apply to the Charity Commissioners, if you did not agree to an arbitration
you had stopped the workmen at the School

record_reviews.summary: Darwin gives Lubbock a second report after visiting Baugh: Baugh had already approached the Commissioners, might proceed in equity court, and contemplated a parish subscription for legal costs. Darwin says persuasion is useless, adds his temporary Baker Street address, and hopes to meet Lubbock’s son at scientific societies.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Baugh and the lawyer are reported voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This continues the Lubbock dispute and has no missing scientific prompt or new paired endpoint in the packet.

evidence.quote: he has actually already called at the office of the Commissioners
He seems very determined, even more than before

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Lubbock to support Huxley’s candidacy for the University of London physiology and comparative anatomy examinership. He lists Huxley’s museum position, lectures, publications, Royal Medal, foreign-language literature and student Gold Medal, then apologizes for missing dinner.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 27 May [1856]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored advocacy note; Huxley’s qualifications are reported by Darwin and Lubbock is the institutional intermediary.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Lubbock response is preserved; this is a recommendation, not a scientific reply.

evidence.quote: My friend, Mr. Huxley F.R.S. is a candidate for the Examinership in Physiology
He has published several papers in the Phil: Transact

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Lubbock for a note, offers to forward it to Wedgwood, and will discuss admission cards. He corrects the misunderstanding that Lubbock wanted furniture, then closes.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 18 Nov [1856]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The underlying Lubbock note and any Wedgwood exchange are not preserved; no broader relationship is inferred.

evidence.quote: I am much obliged for your note, which I will forward to Mr. Wedgwood
I see it was an entire blunder of A. Woods about your wanting the Furniture

issues: All records are boundary probes; most have open 1809 lower XML bounds and are not period-selection eligible. The safe 1843–1846 contexts are retained only as historical comparison, not as 1858–1859 knowledge.
No inline visual nodes were attached to these records. Textual mentions of plates, drawings, specimens or diagrams were recorded as source content without claiming visual inspection.
Institutional minutes, a penitentiary appeal, a proof-correction-like report and third-party observations remain their original source roles.
